We conduct a large-scale survey involving over 1,000 participants, asking them to submit representative tasks that they have actually applied AI to assist with or genuinely intended to accomplish with AI.
After initial quality filtering, we retain over 500 tasks, which are organized into four broad domains: Personal Life, White-Collar Work, Study & Research, and Others.

Given the open-ended nature of xDailyBench, where multiple valid solutions may exist, the rubric defines the task’s success conditions rather than a single reference output, enabling automatic evaluation while preserving solution diversity.

Each criterion corresponds to an explicit or implicit task requirement.
Together, the criteria cover all essential requirements of successful task completion.
The remaining tasks are then cross-reviewed by contributors through a structured manual inspection.
For every task, each rubric criterion is required to achieve an agreement rate of at least 90% between automatic and human judgments across these trials.

xDailyBench is organized into a two-level taxonomy comprising 248 real-world tasks across four C1 domains (including Others) and 51 fine-grained C2 scenarios, providing broad coverage of diverse daily knowledge work.
each task is accompanied by an average of 13.3 binary rubric items, organized into 5 high-level capability dimensions, as detailed in Appendix C
Explicit requirements (70.5%) are directly stated or constrained in the user query.

General implicit requirements (18.5%) are unstated but generally expected for successful task completion, such as verifiability, executability, factuality, appropriate formatting and precision, or domain-specific conventions and professional practices.
User-specific implicit requirements (11.0%) are not explicitly stated and must instead be inferred from the user’s role, background, or contextual information to satisfy their particular needs.
each task is categorized by difficulty level (easy, medium, or hard) based on the contributors’ professional judgment
The scenario distribution is intentionally diverse rather than concentrated in a few dominant categories, with the largest C2 category containing only 16 tasks.
All models receive identical task instructions, tool access, and execution budgets, with a maximum of 120 agent steps per task without any model-specific prompting or human intervention.
For evaluation, we adopt an LLM-as-a-Judge protocol for pure-text responses and an Agent-as-a-Judge protocol for file-based deliverables.
To eliminate judge-side variation, we use GLM-5.1 as the judge model throughout all experiments.
The best models achieve a task-level score of 75.6%, while all models perform substantially worse on implicit than explicit requirements, with gaps no less than 9 percentage points.
Implicit requirements remain a major bottleneck.

Averaged over all evaluated models, Instruction Following (70.7) and Artifact Quality (70.2) achieve the highest scores, followed by Information Understanding (68.2) and Analytical Reasoning (67.6), whereas Quantitative Reasoning is substantially lower at 60.1.

Although Seed-2.1-Evolving and Kimi-K3 obtain the same overall task-level score of 75.6, their capability profiles differ substantially, indicating that similar aggregate performance can mask different underlying strengths and weaknesses.

Evaluates whether the model correctly interprets the task input and relevant contextual information, including user-provided text, files, images, attachments, and other task-specific materials, and identifies the information necessary to complete the task.

Measures whether the model follows explicit user requirements, task constraints, required procedures, and applicable rules or regulations, while avoiding unsupported actions or outputs beyond what the task permits.

Measures the quality and usability of the final deliverable, including completeness, factual correctness, organization, formatting, readability, and whether the produced artifact satisfies the expected output form and task requirements.
Evaluates the correctness of numerical reasoning, including calculations, quantitative comparisons, estimation, data interpretation, and the use of numerical evidence required by the task.

It covers 56 everyday scenarios and 248 authentic, open-ended tasks spanning personal life, work, and study, evaluating end-to-end agent performance on real-world everyday needs under realistic user constraints.

We address the limitations of existing exam-style and professional workflow benchmarks, which often fail to capture ambiguous, personalized, context-dependent requests with no single ground-truth answer.

Evaluation across 11 frontier models shows that the best-performing model achieves only 75.6% task-level performance, while all models exhibit over 9 percentage-point gaps on implicit requirements, highlighting intent inference as a persistent bottleneck for reliable task completion.
The construction of xDailyBench follows a rigorous, multi-stage pipeline that integrates real-user contributions, AI-assisted review, and iterative human quality control .

Tasks are contributed by participants with practical experience using AI tools recruited through a crowdsourcing platform , who submit scenarios identical or similar to those they genuinely encounter in their personal lives, professional workflows, or studies.
The benchmark spans broad daily-use scenarios and attaches a structured rubric and capability labels to every task.
